summary: John the Baptist preaches repentance in the wilderness, baptizes crowds in the Jordan, and points away from himself to the Mightier One who is coming.
key_insight: Asked who he was, John kept saying what he was not: not the Christ, not Elijah, not the Prophet, not even worthy to untie a sandal. The greatest of the prophets called himself only a voice.
story: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, while Annas and Caiaphas were high priests, the word of God came to John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness. {Lk} He went into all the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. {Lk}

“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand!” he proclaimed. {Mt} He was the one Isaiah had spoken of: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the LORD; Make His paths straight.’” Isaiah’s words went on: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.” {Lk} Mark sets beside them the word of Malachi: “Behold, I send My messenger before Your face.” {Mk}

John wore clothing of camel’s hair with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey. Jerusalem, all Judea and all the region around the Jordan went out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. {Mt}

When he saw many Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, {Mt} he said, “Brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Therefore bear fruits worthy of repentance.” Being children of Abraham would not save them; God could raise up children to Abraham from these stones. “And even now the ax is laid to the root of the trees.”

The crowds asked him, “What shall we do then?” He told them that whoever had two tunics should give to the one who had none, and whoever had food should do the same. Tax collectors came too, and he told them, “Collect no more than what is appointed for you.” To soldiers he said, “Do not intimidate anyone or accuse falsely, and be content with your wages.” {Lk}

The people were wondering whether John might be the Christ. {Lk} He answered them all: “I indeed baptize you with water; but One mightier than I is coming, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loose. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” {Lk} The Coming One would clear His threshing floor, gathering the wheat into His barn and burning the chaff with unquenchable fire.

Later, at Bethabara beyond the Jordan, priests and Levites sent from Jerusalem by the Pharisees asked him, “Who are you?” He confessed, “I am not the Christ.” He was not Elijah, and he was not the Prophet. He was only the voice crying in the wilderness. “I baptize with water,” he told them, “but there stands One among you whom you do not know.” {Jn}
differences: Luke alone dates John’s call by the rulers of the day, continues Isaiah’s words to “all flesh shall see the salvation of God,” and records John’s counsel to the crowds, tax collectors and soldiers.
Matthew says John’s “Brood of vipers!” was spoken when he saw Pharisees and Sadducees coming; Luke says he spoke it to the multitudes.
Mark’s account is the shortest. He alone sets Malachi’s “Behold, I send My messenger” beside Isaiah. Matthew and Luke add “and fire” to the promise of the Spirit.
The sandal saying varies: John is not worthy to “carry” them (Matthew), to “stoop down and loose” the strap (Mark), or to “loose” it (Luke and John).
Only John’s Gospel records the delegation from Jerusalem and the Baptist’s denials. It took place after Jesus’ baptism, which John 1:29–34 looks back on.

fit.question: Asked, “Are you Elijah?” John answered, “I am not.” Yet Jesus later said of John, “he is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11:14). Which is right?

points.label: Not Elijah in person
points.text: Malachi had promised, “I will send you Elijah the prophet” (Malachi 4:5), and many expected the prophet himself, taken up to heaven long before, to return. John honestly denied being that man.

points.label: Elijah in his role
points.text: The angel told Zacharias that his son would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). Jesus spoke of the role John filled, and even added, “if you are willing to receive it” (Matthew 11:14). John answered about his person; Jesus spoke about his mission.

fit.note: John answered the question he was asked, and Jesus described the role John filled. Both speak truly.
fit.short: John denied being Elijah returned in person; Jesus meant that John came in Elijah’s spirit and power, as the angel had promised.

fit.question: Matthew says John called the Pharisees and Sadducees a “Brood of vipers!” Luke says he said it to the multitudes. Whom did he address?

points.label: One crowd, one warning
points.text: Matthew says John saw many Pharisees and Sadducees “coming to his baptism,” that is, among the crowds who came. Luke records the warning as the whole crowd heard it; Matthew notes the people it was aimed at most sharply.

points.label: Many sermons
points.text: John preached for months, and Luke says he preached “with many other exhortations” (Luke 3:18). Strong warnings like this were very likely repeated to many audiences.

fit.note: One preacher in a mixed crowd, remembered with a different focus by each writer.
fit.short: The religious leaders were among the crowds. Luke reports the warning as all heard it; Matthew names those it most targeted.

scene.label: The fifteenth year of Tiberius
scene.text: Tiberius became emperor in AD 14. Counted from then, his fifteenth year falls about AD 28–29. If Luke counted from the time Tiberius began to share power with Augustus, about AD 12, it falls about AD 26–27. Either way, Luke ties the gospel to real rulers and real dates.

scene.label: The wilderness of Judea
scene.text: This is the dry, rocky land falling from the hills of Judea down to the Jordan and the Dead Sea. To hear John, people had to leave the city and the temple behind and go out to him, as Israel once met God in the wilderness.

scene.label: Elijah’s clothes
scene.text: Camel’s hair and a leather belt were the marks of Elijah, “A hairy man wearing a leather belt around his waist” (2 Kings 1:8). Locusts were clean food under the law (Leviticus 11:22). John looked and lived like the prophets of old.

scene.label: John’s baptism
scene.text: Jews knew many ritual washings. John’s baptism was different: a single act, received from a prophet, with confession of sins, to prepare for the One who was coming.

scene.label: Tax collectors and soldiers
scene.text: Tax collectors gathered tolls and taxes for the ruling powers and were known for taking more than was due. The soldiers who came to John were probably Jewish troops serving Herod Antipas or local officials rather than Roman legionaries.

witnesses.matthew: Gives John’s message in the same words Jesus will later use: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (3:2; 4:17). Matthew names the Pharisees and Sadducees, beginning the conflict with Israel’s leaders that runs through his Gospel.
witnesses.mark: Starts his whole Gospel here, with no birth story: “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.” In eight quick verses John appears, preaches and points beyond himself to the Mightier One.
witnesses.luke: Dates the moment like a historian, extends Isaiah’s words to “all flesh,” and alone records John’s counsel to ordinary people, tax collectors and soldiers. In Luke, repentance shows up in how people handle clothing, food, money and power.
witnesses.john: Records John’s testimony under questioning. The Baptist says what he is not: not the Christ, not Elijah, not the Prophet. In this Gospel, John is above all a witness: he “came for a witness, to bear witness of the Light” (John 1:7).

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the Mightier One whom even the greatest prophet felt unworthy to serve. He comes to baptize with the Holy Spirit and to separate the wheat from the chaff.
seeing.living: John’s call to repent was specific: share your extra tunic, stop overcharging, do not bully, be content with your pay. Repentance that prepares for Jesus reaches into what we own and how we earn our living. And it begins, as John’s ministry did, by making much of Jesus and little of ourselves.
seeing.ponder: If you asked John, “What shall we do then?”, where would he put his finger in your life?

preaching.big_idea: Prepare for Jesus with repentance that bears fruit in everyday life.
preaching.watch_for: Luke 3:1–2 names seven powerful men: an emperor, a governor, three rulers and two high priests. Then the word of God comes to none of them, but to John in the wilderness.
